questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Choosing a representative from each class
questions.learningObjective: explain what one member of an equivalence class buys a test set
questions.stem: A form accepts a discount code of at most eight characters. A team plans one test per equivalence class of code length. Why pick a single member of each class rather than a handful of arbitrary ones?

options.text: One member per class covers every way the rule can behave, so more of the same class adds no reach
More members of one class can still expose a rule that varies inside that class
options.misconception: believes a rule can change within what was called a single class

options.text: Each chosen member should sit exactly on a class boundary to count as representative
options.misconception: confuses a representative value with a boundary value

options.text: One member per class also measures how often the rule fires across real inputs
options.misconception: thinks a representative doubles as a frequency measurement

questions.explanation: An equivalence class collects every input the rule treats identically, so the rule cannot answer differently for two members of the same class. One member therefore exercises the whole class, and extra members only repeat a verdict already obtained. The tempting pull towards more inputs comes from coverage figures counting lines rather than classes, and a boundary value belongs to a different technique: it sits where the rule changes its answer, so it is the one member of a class worth naming individually.
questions.hint: Ask what two inputs in the same class could tell you that one did not.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Where the boundary between classes sits
questions.learningObjective: state what a chosen class boundary lets a test set assume
questions.stem: A locker accepts numbers from 1 to 20, so its classes split between 20 and 21. What does that split let a test set assume about the values on each side?

options.text: Values on one side behave identically, so a class only needs one member tested to know its answer
A safe set must still try every integer next to the split, since the rule may vary there
options.misconception: believes a rule can vary between neighbours inside one class

options.text: The split is where a loop must stop, so it fixes how many iterations the loop runs
options.misconception: confuses a class boundary with the end of a loop

options.text: Choosing one member per class also certifies the exact values at the split itself
options.misconception: thinks one member per class proves the boundary values

questions.explanation: The point of drawing the split is to record that everything on one side takes the same branch, so a single member stands in for all of them. Neighbouring integers inside a class cannot disagree, which is why the extra inputs buy nothing. Mistaking the split for a loop bound is common because both are written with a comparison, but a class boundary answers a question about the rule while a loop bound answers a question about the data length, and the two can move independently.
questions.hint: Ask whether two values on the same side could ever get different answers.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The three values around one boundary
questions.learningObjective: name the three inputs that expose a fault at one boundary
questions.stem: A booking form accepts values from 5 up to 10, and a team can spend three tests on this rule. Which three values would a fault at the lower limit need?

options.text: 4, 5 and 6, the value just below, the value at the limit, and the one just above
5 and 6, because the limit and the value above it already show the change
options.misconception: believes the value just below the limit cannot matter

options.text: 4 and 7, because one value from each side of the limit is representative
options.misconception: believes one value per side is enough to catch a strict comparison

options.text: 5 and 10, because the first and last accepted values are the rule's boundaries
options.misconception: calls the extremes of a range the boundaries being examined

questions.explanation: A comparison is decided by whether it is strict or loose, and only an input exactly equal to the limit can tell the two apart: with a strict test the limit is rejected, with a loose test it is accepted, and a value either side is accepted or rejected under both. The pair 5 and 6 therefore looks like evidence and is not, because a strict rule passes it. Taking the extremes of the range confuses the ends of the accepted set with the single boundary under study.
questions.hint: Ask which input makes strict and loose comparisons disagree.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a rule fails most often at its edges
questions.learningObjective: explain why faults cluster where a rule changes its answer
questions.stem: A discount rule switches behaviour at a spend of 100, and reported faults of that rule cluster at 100 rather than at 50. Why does the switch attract the bugs?

options.text: The switch is where the comparison decides the answer, so strict against loose flips a whole result
Large amounts are harder to compute exactly, so the arithmetic breaks down near the switch
options.misconception: blames numeric precision for a fault that follows a comparison

options.text: Customers rarely spend near the middle, so faults there stay hidden for longer
options.misconception: attributes the clustering to where inputs happen to be rare

options.text: The switch is the part of the rule that runs most often, so it is the part that wears out
options.misconception: believes a branch fails more often because it executes more often

questions.explanation: Away from the switch the comparison has an obvious answer whatever its exact form, so a strict against loose mistake changes nothing and the test suite stays green. At the switch the two forms disagree, which is the only place the mistake becomes visible in behaviour, and it is also the only place a user is likely to land exactly. Frequency of execution is a red herring: a branch that runs most often is not thereby the branch that is wrong.
questions.hint: Ask where a strict and a loose comparison would give different answers.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Choosing an input that tells two candidates apart
questions.learningObjective: select the input that separates two candidate implementations
questions.stem: Two candidate implementations of the same rule differ in one comparison: one is strict, the other is loose. What kind of input tells them apart in a single run?

options.text: An input equal to the value the comparison names, where the strict form and the loose form part company
A value far above the named value, since that is where the two forms differ most
options.misconception: believes the forms diverge further apart rather than at the point

options.text: A value far below the named value, since the loose form rejects what the strict form keeps
options.misconception: believes the forms disagree away from the comparison point

options.text: Any value at all, provided the same input is run against both candidates in turn
options.misconception: thinks any input separates two candidates if both are run

questions.explanation: A test that must choose between two explanations has to be sensitive to the difference between them, and a single input is sensitive only where the two candidates predict different outputs. For a strict against loose comparison that is exactly the named value, because everywhere else both forms take the same branch. Running both candidates on one unchosen input is the usual way teams waste an afternoon: agreement on that input removes the fault, but the input picked at random is almost never the one that carries the disagreement.
questions.hint: Ask where the two forms predict different outputs, not merely where they both run.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Stating an invariant instead of one expected number
questions.learningObjective: explain what a stated property offers that one expected value does not
questions.stem: Instead of listing expected outputs for a sorting routine, a tester states that the output has the same length as the input and its first value is no larger than its last. What has the tester gained?

options.text: A check that holds for a whole family of inputs, so generated cases can be judged as they arrive
The exact expected output, so each generated case can be compared against a known value
options.misconception: believes a property pins down the precise output for every input

options.text: No need for hand-written cases, since the property covers every input the generator can build
options.misconception: believes a property makes written test cases unnecessary

options.text: Nothing, because the statement only repeats the requirement in different words
options.misconception: assumes a checkable property is the same as restating the requirement

questions.explanation: A stored expected value settles one input, so a new input needs a new stored value written by a person. A property is a statement about a relation that must hold for every member of a family, so the same check can judge any number of inputs, including generated ones nobody thought to write down. The cost is real and worth stating: a property says less about any single input, so a routine can satisfy the property and still be wrong in ways the property does not describe.
questions.hint: Ask how many inputs one stored value settles versus one property.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A generated case that would break the stated property
questions.learningObjective: select the generated case a property can actually distinguish
questions.stem: A routine must leave a list's total unchanged by any shuffle. The generator offers three cases. Which one exposes a routine that quietly drops repeated values while copying?

options.text: The case of three equal values, because only there does the total fall when repeats are removed
The case of three distinct values, because repeats leave the most room for a wrong total
options.misconception: believes distinct values are what catch a fault that removes repeats

options.text: The case of a single zero, because a zero at the front exposes the first slot being overwritten
options.misconception: assumes a leading zero is the discriminating input for a repeat fault

options.text: The case of an empty list, because a zero-length total is the hardest case to compute
options.misconception: believes the empty case is where a repeat-removal fault shows up

questions.explanation: A property check is only as sharp as the cases fed to it, so a generated case earns its place when it separates a correct routine from a wrong one. A routine that removes repeats keeps the total of a list of distinct values, so that case is passed by both and proves nothing. Three equal values make the removal visible, because the correct total and the faulty total differ there and nowhere else in the set. The empty list is the weakest case of all, since almost every fault leaves it unchanged.
questions.hint: Ask which case gives the correct routine and the faulty routine different totals.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A check that passes without testing the rule
questions.learningObjective: explain why a not-null check passes a routine that returns wrong values
questions.stem: A check asserts only that the returned record is not null, and it passes. The routine under test returns a freshly created record whose every field is still at its default. Why did the check pass?

options.text: The assertion looks at a property the rule never promised, so a record full of wrong values still satisfies it
The check ran faster than the routine, so it saw the record before the fields were filled
options.misconception: attributes a passing check to a race with the routine's own work

options.text: The routine did return a record, so a rule about that record's fields is satisfied as well
options.misconception: assumes producing an object satisfies any rule about its contents

options.text: The check declared no expected value, so there was nothing for it to compare and disagree with
options.misconception: believes a check with no expected value reports a pass by design

questions.explanation: An assertion is a claim, and this one claims only that an object came back. The requirement is about the fields inside that object, so a record with every field defaulted is wrong while still satisfying the claim, which is the definition of a check that passes for the wrong reason. The value of such a check is not zero, since it does catch a routine that returns nothing at all, but it is far below what its presence in the suite suggests, and a green run then reads as far stronger evidence than it is.
questions.hint: Ask which property the requirement actually names.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The change that makes a weak check bite
questions.learningObjective: choose the change that turns a shape check into a check of the rule
questions.stem: A check asserts only that a discounted total is not null. Which change turns it into a check of the rule the routine was written for?

options.text: Assert the exact total for a fixed input, so a wrong figure has to fail the check to pass
Run the check twice, since a second run may produce a different figure to compare
options.misconception: believes repeating a check supplies the missing expected value

options.text: Also assert the figure is not empty, which covers the shape as well as the value
options.misconception: adds a second shape check and treats that as a stronger claim

options.text: Guard the inputs first, so bad figures cannot reach the check in the first place
options.misconception: assumes validating inputs checks the routine's output rule

questions.explanation: A shape check asks whether anything came back; a rule check asks what came back. Adding the exact expected figure for a fixed input is what closes the gap, because a discounted total of the wrong size is now a failure rather than a pass. Rerunning the same check cannot help, since without a stated expectation both runs accept whatever the routine produces. Guarding the inputs is worth doing anyway, but it is a different claim: it says the routine was called fairly, not that it answered correctly.
questions.hint: Ask what the check must know to have a verdict other than yes.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Choosing a stub for the question being asked
questions.learningObjective: name the double that suits a question about a computed band
questions.stem: A test needs a routine that asks the system clock for today's date. The question under test is which discount band that date falls into. Which double fits?

options.text: A stub that hands back a fixed date, because the test needs to control that input rather than watch the call
A mock that fails unless the clock is read exactly once, to count the calls the routine makes
options.misconception: believes the question under test is how often the clock is read

options.text: A fake that keeps a real calendar in memory, so the routine under test stays untouched
options.misconception: believes a working replacement is needed when only the date must be fixed

options.text: A spy that writes every call to a log the test inspects once the run is over
options.misconception: believes recording the call is what the band question needs

questions.explanation: A double is chosen by the question, not by habit. A stub exists to supply an input the test wants to dictate, and a fixed date dictates the clock exactly, so the band the routine picks is a predictable result. A mock or a spy also observes, which adds a claim about how the routine used its collaborator, and that claim is not the one being asked here. A fake goes further again by supplying real behaviour, which is the right choice when the collaborator's own logic is part of what is under test.
questions.hint: Ask whether the test needs the clock dictated, watched, or replaced by real logic.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why replacing every collaborator hides a design problem
questions.learningObjective: read the number of doubles as evidence about the routine's shape
questions.stem: A check replaces eight collaborators with doubles and asserts the exact order of their calls. The routine under test reads badly and the check breaks whenever two calls are swapped. What does the number of doubles reveal?

options.text: The routine decides too much itself, so the check has to police the order of its own decisions
The check has grown too large and belongs split across several smaller check files
options.misconception: reads the number of doubles as a file-size problem

options.text: The chosen double library is the wrong one, and another would cost less to set up
options.misconception: blames the testing tool rather than what the routine does

options.text: The routine is quick and the check is slow, so the timings should be measured and compared
options.misconception: reads a design smell as a performance problem to profile

questions.explanation: A routine that only needs one or two collaborators can be checked through the values it returns, and a handful of doubles at most. The moment a check has to name eight collaborators and their order, it is holding a second copy of the routine's design, and that copy breaks every time someone tidies the order without changing behaviour. Over-mocking is therefore a design signal about the routine, not a testing failure, and the repair is to move a decision out of the routine rather than to assert the new order more carefully.
questions.hint: Ask what the check has to encode that the routine's own code does not already say.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why arranging, acting and asserting are kept in order
questions.learningObjective: explain what the fixed three-step order buys a reader
questions.stem: A check builds a customer record, calls the routine that charges it, then asserts on the balance. Why is the order of those three steps worth keeping fixed?

options.text: A reader can see at a glance what was prepared, what ran, and what was judged, so a failure is easy to place
The order decides which assertion fires first when several of them would fail
options.misconception: believes step order determines which failure gets reported

options.text: Arranging the inputs first is the cheapest order, so the check runs faster than the others
options.misconception: believes the step order is chosen for the speed it produces

options.text: Asserting before acting would surface the fault sooner inside the run
options.misconception: believes asserting earlier in the run reports the fault sooner

questions.explanation: The three steps are the shape of every check worth reading, and fixing their order means a reader never has to work out which statements set the stage and which ones judge the result. When a check fails, the position of the failing assertion immediately tells the reader whether the routine or the setup is suspect. None of that depends on which assertion fires first, since a run reports every failure anyway, and arranging first has nothing to do with speed because all three steps happen once regardless of order.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can tell from where a failing assertion sits.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Shared test data that outlives one test
questions.learningObjective: trace how one check leaves state that decides another check's result
questions.stem: Several checks share one in-memory list, and the first of them sorts that list in place. A later check asserts the list is still in insertion order and fails. What is the mechanism?

options.text: The first check left the shared list reordered, so the later one reads state that it never created
The sort is not stable, so equal entries swap and the order can never be relied on
options.misconception: blames sort stability for a failure caused by leftover state

options.text: The runner executes the checks in an order nobody wrote down, so the second ran early
options.misconception: blames an unknown run order rather than the leftover data

options.text: The list outgrew its capacity, so the earliest entries were silently dropped
options.misconception: invents a capacity fault that the scenario never states

questions.explanation: A check's result should follow from the inputs that check supplied, and a shared mutable object breaks that: the second check asserts about data whose order was decided by the first. The failure is order-dependent rather than random, which is what makes it so confusing in a large suite, since it appears only when both checks run in one session. Rebuilding the data in the second check's own setup removes the dependency, and a suite that hands each check its own copy can be run in any order at all.
questions.hint: Ask who last wrote to the list before the failing assertion read it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A check that changes verdict with the calendar
questions.learningObjective: identify the unstated input a time-dependent check depends on
questions.stem: A check asserts that a renewal reminder is sent 30 days before an expiry date. It passes in March and fails in December with the same stored data. What has the check made itself depend on?

options.text: Today's date, since the gap between today and the expiry date decides whether the reminder is due
The length of the month, because a shorter month leaves fewer days for the thirty to fit in
options.misconception: blames month lengths for a result that follows the current date

options.text: The time zone of the machine that runs the check, since it reads the clock differently
options.misconception: blames a machine's time zone for a verdict that follows the date

options.text: The version of the reminder library the check happens to be linked against that day
options.misconception: blames the linked library for a verdict that follows the clock

questions.explanation: A check that reads the clock during the run has taken the current date as an input without naming it, so its verdict is a function of when it ran as well as of the stored data. March and December sit at opposite ends of the year, which is exactly the kind of gap that turns a hidden dependency into an intermittent failure somebody blames on the environment. Passing that date in as a parameter, or stubbing the clock, moves the dependency into the setup where a reader can see it.

questions.topic: A check that depends on the machine's language settings
questions.learningObjective: explain what a locale-sensitive assertion is really claiming
questions.stem: A check parses the text 1,5 and expects the decimal one and a half. It passes on a machine set to English and fails on a machine set to German. What is the check really asserting?

options.text: One machine's number format, rather than any rule about which characters the input may hold
That the parser accepts every decimal spelling used anywhere in the world
options.misconception: believes one machine's format stands for every regional format

options.text: That the two machines happen to run different builds of the parser
options.misconception: blames a build difference for a difference in language settings

options.text: That a comma is an illegal character in any decimal input on any machine
options.misconception: generalises one machine's format into a rule for every machine

questions.explanation: The check did not state a rule about the text; it recorded whatever one machine's settings happened to produce and froze that as the expectation. Running it elsewhere then reports a difference in environment rather than a fault in the routine, and the failure lands in the wrong place entirely. questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a fixed random seed does not prove
questions.learningObjective: separate what a fixed seed guarantees from what it cannot show
questions.stem: A check fixes the random seed, reruns, and receives the same two hundred rows every time. The team concludes the routine is correct. What has that conclusion failed to establish?

options.text: That the routine is right on the inputs that one fixed sequence never produced
That the routine would give the same answer on a different machine with the same seed
options.misconception: believes a fixed seed makes a result independent of the machine

options.text: That the source of the random numbers themselves is free of defects
options.misconception: believes a repeatable sequence validates the generator behind it

options.text: That every input the routine could ever receive has now been covered at least once
options.misconception: believes one fixed sequence stands in for the whole input space

questions.explanation: A fixed seed buys reproducibility, which is genuinely valuable: the failing case can be named and replayed instead of hunted for. What it cannot buy is reach, because the same seed produces the same two hundred rows and no others, so a fault that needs a different row stays invisible however many times the check runs green. Reproducibility and coverage are separate properties, and the strongest arrangement is a fixed seed for the failures worth keeping plus a varying seed for the sweeps meant to find new ones.
questions.hint: Ask how many distinct rows a fixed seed can ever generate.

questions.topic: A comparison that hides which side is wrong
questions.learningObjective: explain what is lost when both sides of an assertion share a source
questions.stem: A check computes the expected total by running a second copy of the same arithmetic, then asserts that the two totals are equal. When it fails, what has the developer lost?

options.text: Any way to tell which side is wrong, because the same misreading produced both totals
The list of rows that differ, which a total comparison cannot show even when it is fair
options.misconception: blames the loss of row detail rather than the shared source

options.text: The correct total itself, since neither side of the assertion states one
options.misconception: blames the missing correct figure rather than the shared source

options.text: The order the rows were read in, which any total comparison necessarily discards
options.misconception: blames row order for a mismatch between two totals

questions.explanation: An assertion is only informative when its two sides can come apart, and here they cannot: the expected value comes from a second reading of the same requirement, so a misreading appears on both sides and cancels. The failure then says only that the two disagree, which is no more than the disagreement itself. Stating a small case as a literal, and deriving a large expected value by some independent route, restores the ability to say which side is wrong.

questions.topic: The cost of a large golden file
questions.learningObjective: explain why a large stored output defeats the purpose of a comparison
questions.stem: A check compares generated output against a stored copy of four thousand lines. Changing one heading makes the stored copy forty lines longer. What does that say about the check?

options.text: The failure report is mostly shifted lines, so a real change is buried in noise a reader must skip past
The stored copy has fallen out of date and should be rebuilt before every run
options.misconception: blames staleness rather than the size of the failure report

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A relation between two runs instead of one fixed answer
questions.learningObjective: name the kind of evidence a relation between inputs provides
questions.stem: For a routine that finds the largest of a list, a tester checks that the value found for a reversed copy is the same. What kind of check is that?

options.text: A relation between two related inputs, checked instead of one stored answer for each input
A boundary check, because reversing moves the largest value to a different edge
options.misconception: reads a reversal as a boundary case on the range

options.text: A coverage check, because reversing reaches a different branch of the routine
options.misconception: reads a metamorphic relation as branch coverage

options.text: A regression check, because the value must match the one recorded on the last run
options.misconception: reads a metamorphic relation as a stored baseline

questions.explanation: A stored answer settles one input and needs a person to write the next one, while a relation is a statement about how two inputs must relate, so it applies to any input at all. That is what makes it useful on generated data and what lets it catch a fault the stored answers happened to miss. The limit is worth keeping in view: a relation says the two answers are related without saying what either should be, so a routine that is wrong in the same way on both inputs can still satisfy it.

questions.topic: Separating a wrong answer from a late one
questions.learningObjective: select the evidence that tells a slow result from a wrong result
questions.stem: A report arrives after the deadline every morning and shows the right figures. Which piece of evidence separates a late answer from a wrong one?

options.text: Give the same report a longer allowance on a smaller input and see whether the figures stay correct
Read the log, since a wrong answer always leaves a warning in the log file
options.misconception: assumes every wrong answer writes a warning of its own

options.text: Check the schedule, because a late run means the input file has been corrupted
options.misconception: infers input corruption from the lateness of a run

options.text: Ask the operator, since only the person running the report can tell the two apart

If the figures stay right when given longer, the routine is slow rather than faulty, and the work belongs on the time it takes. Insisting that a wrong answer must announce itself in a log confuses a good practice with a guarantee, because a routine that quietly returns a plausible wrong total writes no warning at all.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Repeated rows in a test table
questions.learningObjective: count the rows in a test table that add no new class
questions.stem: A refund routine rejects requests older than 30 days. Its test table holds 12, 20, 29, 30, 31, 45, 0, 29, 30, 15, 45, 5. How many of these rows repeat a value already in the table?

options.text: 3, because 29, 30 and 45 each appear a second time and add no new behaviour
2, because only the values either side of 30 are worth repeating in a table like this
options.misconception: counts only the values near the boundary as the repeated ones

options.text: 4, because every value in the second half of the table is a repeat of the first
options.misconception: treats the whole second half as duplicated values

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Halving a list of saved builds to one fault
questions.learningObjective: count the test runs a halving search needs to isolate one build
questions.stem: Eight saved builds are marked, where true means the run passed. Trace this to find how many builds it has to try before it can name the first failing one. marks <- [true, true, false, false, false, true, true, true]. DEFINE firstBad(marks): lo <- 0. hi <- LENGTH(marks) - 1. runs <- 0. WHILE lo < hi { mid <- (lo + hi) DIV 2. runs <- runs + 1. IF marks[mid] = true { lo <- mid + 1 } ELSE { hi <- mid } }. RETURN runs. DISPLAY firstBad(marks).

options.misconception: counts the halvings of seven candidates rather than of eight
counts every build tried by checking the boundary separately
counts the builds after the first one rather than the builds tried

questions.explanation: The search takes the middle build, index 3, which fails, so the upper bound drops to 3; the middle of 0 to 3 is 1, which passes, so the lower bound rises to 2; the middle of 2 to 3 is 2, which fails, so the bounds meet at the first failing build. That is three builds tried out of eight, and the halving is what makes it three rather than seven. What the search proves is narrow: it names the first build that failed, not which line inside it did it, and the developer still has to compare that build with the one before it.
questions.hint: Take the middle index first, then work inward from whichever side the answer moved.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Objects still reachable after each batch
questions.learningObjective: count the objects a routine still holds after a run of batches
questions.stem: A service runs five batches of work, each creating three objects, and one batch has two of its objects released. Trace this to find how many objects are still held after the fifth batch. batches <- 5. made <- 3. retained <- 0. log <- []. b <- 1. WHILE b <= batches { retained <- retained + made. IF b = 2 { retained <- retained - 2 }. log <- APPEND(log, retained). b <- b + 1 }. DISPLAY log[4].

options.misconception: adds all fifteen objects and ignores the two that were released
subtracts the released objects from every batch rather than from one
reports the objects held after the first batch alone

questions.explanation: The held count after each batch is 3, 4, 7, 10 and 13, so the fifth leaves 13 of the 15 objects still reachable. The shape of the list is the finding rather than the final number: it rises by three every batch except the second, where it dips by two and then resumes climbing, and a sequence that never settles is what a leak looks like from outside. A routine that released everything it created would hold the same small number after every batch, so the plateau, not the total, is the thing to watch for.
questions.hint: Work out the held count after each batch in turn and read the last one.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: How much of a stored copy one change invalidates
questions.learningObjective: count the lines of a stored copy that one change puts in doubt
questions.stem: A report has four sections, and only the third is a long block of 120 lines. A change renames the first section's heading. Trace this to find how many lines of the stored copy a reviewer must read to check it. widths <- [1, 1, 120, 1]. DEFINE linesInDoubt(widths, renamed): total <- 0. i <- 0. WHILE i < LENGTH(widths) { IF i = renamed { total <- total + 1 } ELSE IF widths[i] > 1 { total <- total + widths[i] } i <- i + 1 }. RETURN total. DISPLAY linesInDoubt(widths, 0).

options.misconception: counts only the renamed line and ignores the shifted block behind it
counts the shifted block without the renamed line itself
counts the renamed line and its caption rather than the whole block

questions.explanation: Renaming the heading puts its own one line in doubt, and everything in the long third section moves down by a line as a result, so 120 more lines are in doubt: 121 in total. Almost none of them changed in any meaningful sense, which is the whole cost of keeping one long stored copy. A reader who has to sift 121 lines to find a single renamed heading will learn to skim the report, and a report nobody reads is not protecting anything.
questions.hint: Count the renamed line, then add every long block that shifts because of it.

questions.topic: A boundary input and the verdict it would produce
questions.learningObjective: pair a boundary input with the outcome that would expose a wrong comparison
questions.stem: A capacity rule accepts loads of 1 to 8 items. Which option pairs a test input with the outcome that would expose a wrong comparison at the upper limit?

options.text: Load 8, expecting it accepted, because a strict comparison would refuse it and the fault would show at once
Load 8, expecting it refused, since a stated limit names the first value that is turned away
options.misconception: believes a written limit names the first rejected value

options.text: Load 1, expecting it refused, since zero items is the boundary just below the range
options.misconception: picks a boundary outside the stated range as the one to test

options.text: Load 4, expecting it accepted, since the middle of a range is the most representative value to try
options.misconception: believes an interior value can expose a boundary fault

Expecting a refusal at 8 would pass both the correct rule and the faulty one, which is the trap worth naming: a stored expectation has to come from the requirement, not from a hunch about where a limit falls. A value from the middle cannot expose a comparison the value never reaches.
questions.hint: Ask which input the strict and the loose forms answer differently about.

questions.topic: A double and the check that proves the outcome
questions.learningObjective: pair a double with a check that fails when a retry is removed
questions.stem: A check must show that a routine retries once and still reports success. Which option pairs the double with the check that would fail if the retry were removed?

options.text: A stub that refuses the first call, checking that the routine still reports the eventual success
A mock that records every call, checking the recorded order against a stored order
options.misconception: confuses proving the outcome with proving the order of the calls

options.text: A fake that stores rows in memory, checking the stored rows against a stored count
options.misconception: believes proving an outcome needs a working replacement

options.text: A spy that watches the connection, checking that more than one request was sent
options.misconception: measures the traffic instead of the routine's own decision

A fake that really stores rows is more machinery than the question needs.

questions.topic: A cause and the repair that removes it
questions.learningObjective: pair a leaked-state cause with the repair that removes the dependency
questions.stem: One check fails when run after the totals check and passes on its own. Which option names both the cause and the repair?

A clock read during the earlier check, and freezing the clock for both of the checks
options.misconception: blames the clock when the carried-over data is what the two checks share

options.text: A slow machine, and moving the failing check to the start of the suite
options.misconception: hides the leak by reordering the suite instead of repairing the data

options.misconception: reaches for a load-time fault when the failure follows run order

Reordering the suite only hides the dependency until the next person adds a check in front of it.

questions.topic: A property and the case that breaks it
questions.learningObjective: pair a property with a generated case that would break it
questions.stem: Which option pairs a property a tester could state with a generated case that would break it?

options.text: A list's total is unchanged by shuffling, and three equal values against a routine that drops repeats
A list's total is unchanged by shuffling, and three distinct values against that same routine
options.misconception: picks a case the property cannot tell apart from a correct routine

options.text: A list's first value is its smallest after sorting, and a list whose smallest sits last
options.misconception: states a property the generated case does not test

options.text: A list's length is unchanged by shuffling, and two equal values against that same routine
options.misconception: pairs a length property with a case about repeated values

A property about length is a fine property; it simply has nothing to say about repeats being lost.

questions.topic: The pair of runs that shows a fix worked
questions.learningObjective: pair the two runs that make a fix claim falsifiable
questions.stem: A developer changes one comparison and a previously failing check now passes. Which pair of steps is the strongest evidence that the change is what fixed it?

options.text: See the check fail on the code as it was, then see it pass on the code as it is now
Run the new code twice, since a second pass rules out a timing accident in the first
options.misconception: believes a repeated pass is the same as having seen the failure

options.text: Run the whole suite on the new code, since a clean run settles the change on its own
options.misconception: accepts a clean run as proof without the paired failure

options.text: Compare the coverage figures, since more covered lines show the change is the right one
options.misconception: substitutes a coverage number for behavioural evidence

questions.explanation: A claim that a change fixed a fault is only checkable if the same check can be seen failing without that change, which is why the before run matters as much as the after one. A clean suite says the change did not break anything, and a repeated pass says the pass is not an accident of timing, but neither says the change is responsible for the failure disappearing. Coverage figures describe what was executed rather than what came out, so they cannot carry that weight.
questions.hint: Ask what the change would look like if it had fixed nothing at all.

questions.topic: Instrumentation for a fault seen only under load
questions.learningObjective: pair a probe with the reading that would show a lost update
questions.stem: A fault appears on about one request in fifty and only when the service is busy. Which option pairs the instrumentation with the reading that would show what is going wrong?

options.text: A probe that records the shared total each time it is read, and a report where the total went backwards
A log of the final total on every request, and a report where the totals differ from the sum of the parts
options.misconception: reads a symptom log as evidence of the ordering fault

options.text: A snapshot of retained objects, and a report showing them rising through the load run
options.misconception: reaches for a leak snapshot when the fault is a lost update

options.text: A stack trace from the first failure, and a report naming the method that threw
options.misconception: relies on a trace for a fault that never throws

A final-total log shows the symptom and a memory snapshot shows a different fault altogether, and a stack trace is useless here because nothing throws.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be recorded that one request's own result cannot show.

questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that reduce a report to a smallest failing case

Write down the exact inputs that were used and the figures that came out
Turn that case into a permanent check before any of the code is changed
Remove one input at a time, keeping only those the failure depends on

questions.explanation: Nothing can be removed until it is known what was there, so the inputs and the wrong figures are written down first. Each input then goes in turn, and one that makes no difference comes out while the rest stay, which leaves a case small enough to reason about and to hand to someone else. Only once the case stands alone is it worth writing as a check, because a check that changes shape every time a line is removed is not a check anybody can rely on.

Find the behaviour the check was originally written to protect
Put the routine back as it was and confirm the check is green again
Break that behaviour deliberately, in the smallest way the check ought to notice

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a stub fits a question about a computed value
questions.learningObjective: explain why a stub suits a band calculation better than a mock
questions.stem: A check must show that a renewal reminder is sent 30 days before an expiry date, without waiting 30 days to find out. Explain why a stub that returns a fixed date suits this better than a mock that records the calls.

answer.exemplar: The rule under test is which band a date falls into, so the only thing the test needs from the clock is a value it can dictate: hand back a date either side of a band edge and the band's name is a settled result. A mock also watches how the routine used the clock, so it makes an extra claim, that the clock is read exactly once, and that claim is a second thing to maintain for no gain here. The mock is not wrong, it is answering a different question, and a test that carries an unasked claim fails for a reason the author has to work out again from scratch. Recording the date the routine passed down and letting the check compare that against the date the fixture meant to give would use the mock for what it is good at, but for a question about which band a fixed date lands in, a stub that returns the date is enough.

questions.explanation: A double is chosen by the question, and this question is about which band a date lands in, which is a question about the value the clock hands back. The mechanism worth stating is that a stub fixes an input and a mock adds a claim about how that input was used, so the mock's extra claim has to be maintained for no benefit here. It is also worth saying what the stub does not buy, namely a check on the date the routine actually passed down, which is a separate concern.
questions.hint: Ask what the check is trying to learn about the routine, not about the clock.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: How shared data makes a verdict depend on order
questions.learningObjective: explain how a shared object makes one check's verdict depend on another
questions.stem: Two checks share one list object, and the first sorts it in place while the second asserts the original order. Explain how this makes the second verdict depend on run order, and what single change removes the dependency.

answer.exemplar: The second check never made the list it asserts about. It found the shared list already sorted, because the first check sorted it in place and never put it back, so its verdict is a function of what ran before it as much as of its own setup. Move the checks around and the failure moves with them, which is why the same suite is green on one machine and red on another. Rebuilding the list inside the second check's own setup makes the verdict follow from its own inputs, and once every check owns its data the order stops mattering at all. Sorting a copy instead would also work, but it leaves the shared list in a state the next check still inherits, so the fix belongs in the setup rather than in the sorting.

questions.explanation: The second check's verdict is decided by data whose last writer was the first check, so the result follows the session rather than the check, and the suite's order becomes part of its specification. Rebuilding the data in the second check's own setup is the change that removes it, because then every verdict follows from inputs that check supplied. Sorting a copy would only move the problem to the next check in the session.
questions.hint: Ask who last wrote to the list before the failing assertion read it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a fixed seed guarantees and what it does not
questions.learningObjective: separate the guarantee a fixed seed gives from the coverage it cannot give
questions.stem: A generated check fixes its seed and produces the same two hundred cases on every run, yet a fault reaches production. Explain what a fixed seed guarantees and what it cannot establish.

answer.exemplar: A fixed seed makes the sequence of cases a function of the seed rather than of the clock or the machine, so a failure found on one run can be replayed exactly on the next, with the same inputs in the same order. That is what makes a failing case worth writing down: it stays a failing case, and a change can be tried against it and judged. What the seed cannot do is widen the search, because the same seed produces the same cases and no others, so a fault that needs an input this sequence never generated stays invisible however many times the check reports success. The two properties are separate, and the useful arrangement is a fixed seed for the cases worth keeping and a varying seed for the sweeps meant to find new ones.

questions.explanation: A fixed seed collapses a run into a function of the seed alone, so the same inputs come back in the same order and a failure can be replayed rather than hunted for; that is the guarantee, and it is a real one. It says nothing about reach, because the same seed yields the same cases and no others, so a fault needing a case this sequence never produced survives every green run. Reach and reproducibility are separate properties and a suite needs both from different runs.
questions.hint: Ask how many distinct cases one fixed seed can produce over any number of runs.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a search over build history does and does not prove
questions.learningObjective: state what halving a build history settles and what it leaves open
questions.stem: Ten saved builds exist, the first passes and the remaining nine all fail. Explain what a halving search over that history establishes, and what it cannot establish about the change that caused the fault.

answer.exemplar: Ten saved builds with only the first passing means the fault entered somewhere in the other nine, and halving that set finds the first failing build in at most four tries, which is a quarter of the work of trying them in order. What the search establishes is exactly that: one build is the boundary between passing and failing, so the change between it and the one before it contains the fault. It establishes nothing about the line, the condition, or even the file, because a build is a snapshot of many changes and the culprit is among all of them. The proof it does offer is negative and still worth having, since every build from the failing one onwards shares the fault, which rules out the earlier ones outright.

questions.explanation: Halving finds the first failing build in at most four tries, so it cuts the search from nine builds to four, and what it establishes is a boundary: everything from that build onwards shares the fault and everything before it does not. It cannot say which line or file inside that build did it, because a build is a snapshot of many changes, so the work of the search is what narrows the diff afterwards rather than what finishes the job. That negative result is still worth having, since it rules the earlier builds out for good.
questions.hint: Ask what a build boundary rules out, and what it says about the line inside it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: How a relation finds a fault a stored answer would miss
questions.learningObjective: explain how a relation between inputs exposes a fault a stored answer misses
questions.stem: A tester checks that a list's total is unchanged when the list is reversed, instead of storing one expected total per input. Explain how that relation can expose a fault, and what it will not tell you.

answer.exemplar: A stored answer settles one input and needs a person to write the next, so a fault that only shows up on an input nobody chose is not caught at all. A relation sidesteps that by making a statement about how two inputs must relate, and any input the generator produces can be put to it, which is why hundreds of cases can be judged by one sentence. Here reversing the list must leave the total alone, and a routine that overwrites one slot while copying breaks that on some arrangements and not others, so the check finds a fault no stored number for that input would have. The limit is the same one the relations share: they say the two answers are related without saying what either should be, so a routine that is wrong the same way both times can still satisfy them.

questions.explanation: A stored answer covers one input and needs a person to supply the next, so a fault that only appears on an unchosen input is never reached. A relation replaces the stored number with a statement about how two inputs must relate, which any generated input can be put to, and the reversal here is exposed because a routine that overwrites a slot while copying breaks the total on some arrangements. The cost is precision: a relation says the two answers are related, never what either should be, so it needs pairing with a stored figure or a second relation to pin a value down.
questions.hint: Ask what a relation knows about the pair that a stored figure would have known.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a check that cannot fail is worse than a loud failure
questions.learningObjective: explain why a check that cannot fail is more damaging than a failing one
questions.stem: A check has passed every day for two years, and when the routine is deliberately broken it still passes. Explain why this is worse than a check that has been failing loudly, and what would make it worth trusting again.

answer.exemplar: A check that has been failing is producing evidence: it names a rule, it points at a place, and it asks for a change. A check that passes for the wrong reason produces the opposite, because a green run is read as a claim that the rule is covered, and a team that believes it will stop looking. Silence is worse than noise here, since a red check is something somebody has to deal with and a check that cannot fail is something nobody revisits. Deliberately breaking the behaviour the check was written for is what turns the claim into a fact, and putting the routine back afterwards shows the check is reading the behaviour and not something nearby. Without that demonstration the check is decoration, however long it has been green.

questions.explanation: A failing check is evidence, because it names a rule, points at a place and demands a change, and a loud failure is something a team has to deal with. A check that cannot fail produces silence where a claim of coverage should be, and the team reads the silence as proof, so the search for a real fault stops. Deliberately breaking the behaviour it was written for is the only way to turn that claim into a fact, and restoring the routine afterwards shows the check reads the behaviour rather than its surroundings.
questions.hint: Ask what a green run from a check that cannot fail tells the team to stop doing.
